li.a: Balkan Insight: 'Only Profit': Decoding Greek Organised Crime
The National Herald: Letter from Athens, Murder, Incorporated
Data Journalists: Greek Mafia, Nine years of turmoil
International Press Institute: Who killed Greek journalist Giorgos Karaivaz?

content.p: "Greek mafia" is a phrase that Greek newspapers use for the gangs that run protection rackets, nightclubs, fuel smuggling and contract killings around Athens. It is a label rather than the name of an organisation. Sofia Vidali, a professor of criminology at Panteion University in Athens, told Balkan Insight that "the most appropriate term is 'organised crime'". The Organized Crime Index describes the Greek groups as less hierarchical than traditional mafias.

What gives the label its weight is a run of shootings. A National Herald report in January 2024 counted at least 23 murders since 2017, which police read as part of a turf war over extortion and the illegal fuel and cigarette trade in Attica. The courts have so far acquitted the defendants in two of the best-known proceedings, and the IPI says 90 to 95 per cent of organised-crime murders in Greece remain unsolved.

The Organized Crime Index, which scores countries on criminal markets and state responses, says the groups often called the Greek Mafia have changed under economic and police pressure, with smaller organisations merging into larger ones. It says that several major organisations now operate in Athens and share out power through agreements between their leaders. Its assessment lists drug trafficking, arms dealing, extortion, money laundering and control of nightclubs among their activities. It also says convicted leaders are believed to keep running their business from inside prison.

A former Greek police officer who spoke to Balkan Insight on condition of anonymity put the shift this way: in the 1990s, criminal organisations were bound by geographical boundaries, but "now, there is no longer a geographical limit; there is only profit." The same report says the groups have forged links across the Balkans.

The Index also says that foreign groups, including ethnic Albanian, Serbo-Montenegrin, Russian, Georgian and Italian ones, are influential in Greece and often work with Greek groups in smuggling. Greek nationals, it says, usually keep control of domestic markets, above all extortion and arms trafficking. It describes fuel smuggling as a market over which the Greek mafia exerts considerable control, in combination with tax fraud and money laundering.

The case known as the "Greek Mafia" case concerns an alleged protection scheme from 2015 and 2016. In December 2016 Yiannis Roubatis, then director of the National Intelligence Service (EYP), sent a 70-page report to the Supreme Court prosecutor. According to Data Journalists, which summarised it, the report described a racket covering brothels, strip clubs, gambling dens and casinos. It named businessman Dimitris Malamas as the network's "treasurer" and as closely linked to Spyros Papachristou, a retired officer of the police special-operations unit EKAM.

The report, as Data Journalists describes it, tied the network to 300 gambling clubs, 300 casinos and 350 brothels, each paying a fixed monthly sum: 1,000 euros for a brothel, 1,500 for a studio, and 5,000 to 7,000 for a gambling club. The court that later heard the misdemeanour charges recorded that part of the payments was "demanded and collected by active police officers serving in various police stations", among them Omonia, Kolonos, Neos Kosmos, Kypseli, Patision and Agios Panteleimonas. Those officers, the court noted, had not been identified.

The prosecution then ran into its own evidence. Police internal-affairs officers were given the task of transcribing the intelligence service's recordings. Their former head, retired Major General Ilias Kosivakis, told prosecutors the recordings amounted to 106,000 phone calls, far more than anti-corruption prosecutors had foreseen. In June 2022, with the statute of limitations approaching, a trial of the misdemeanour charges began before a three-member appeals court, with 17 defendants, among them retired and serving senior police officers.

During the hearings the court ruled that many of the recordings had been made without the prosecutor's authorisation that the law requires, and set them aside. Prosecutor Panagiotis Meidanis told the court that "the evidence in the case file remained essentially non-existent" after more than five years of preliminary investigation and asked for acquittals. In January 2023 the court acquitted all 17, some unanimously and some by majority.

A separate file on felony charges stayed open. In October 2024, according to Data Journalists, First Instance Prosecutor Minas-Alexandros Kaloudis proposed to the Judicial Council that eight of 21 defendants be sent to trial for offences including forming and joining a criminal organisation, racketeering as an accomplice and bribery of public officials. His recommendation described a hierarchy topped by serving and retired police officers, and named Malamas as the organisation's "leader-director". When Data Journalists published in March 2025, the council had not ruled. These are allegations in a prosecutor's proposal, not findings of a court.
content.h2: The people around the file who were shot
content.p: Data Journalists notes that several people who had been under intelligence surveillance in 2015 to 2017 were murdered while the case was under judicial investigation.

Papachristou was shot outside a tavern in Pallini on 1 May 2018. The homicide investigation later stumbled over his two mobile phones. According to Data Journalists, they sat in a drawer at police headquarters in the summer of 2020, and when the file went to prosecutors in 2021 it held no messages from them. The head of the homicide squad at the time was charged with misconduct and tried in December 2024, and was acquitted despite the prosecutor's call for a conviction. Data Journalists says he has since moved to a key post in the intelligence service.

Malamas was killed in October 2019 while sitting in his car at a red light in Haidari, shot by assassins on a motorcycle who used a Kalashnikov. Dimitris Kapetanakis, known as "Kapes" and an underworld figure for decades, was shot with 28 Kalashnikov rounds on Ymittos Street in Vrilissia on 9 December 2020, according to the same report.
content.h2: A journalist's killing and a trial without convictions
content.p: Giorgos Karaivaz, a crime reporter who had run the website bloko.gr since 2009, was shot outside his home in Alimos on 9 April 2021 by two men on a scooter, according to the International Press Institute, which counted ten bullets. The IPI wrote that he was due to testify in a major case against the Greek mafia, and that people close to him believe he was killed to stop him. The then citizen protection minister, Michalis Chrysochoidis, called the killing "a heinous crime against the freedom of the press".

On 28 April 2023, a month before national elections, two brothers were arrested. The IPI gave their ages as 40 and 48, while Data Journalists says 41 and 49; the sources differ. They were held in pretrial detention for 15 months before the trial opened on 26 June 2024 before the Athens Mixed Jury Court of three judges and four jurors. The prosecution's case rested partly on camera footage of the older brother's company van, a white vehicle used in his disinfection business, in the victim's neighbourhood on the day before the killing and on the day itself; the accused said he had been handing out flyers.

The prosecutor asked for guilty verdicts on both, arguing that organised-crime cases often rest on strong circumstantial evidence. The court acquitted them, by 5 to 2 for one brother and 6 to 1 for the other. Data Journalists reports that the court found the evidence did not convincingly prove guilt.

Evidence trouble surfaced during the trial. A prosecutor said a CD holding data from Karaivaz's phone had been destroyed, apparently with a stapler. The IPI said the family's lawyers argued the disc had been recorded as "examined and read" though nobody officially saw it. The journalist's mother and sister appealed the acquittal to the Supreme Court. The IPI's view was that nobody had been punished, neither the gunmen nor whoever ordered the killing; Greek police sources told it the investigation continues.

A different line of killings began to draw attention at the start of 2024. Vangelis Zampounis, known as Zampon, 44, was shot dead at a petrol station in Athens in January 2024. The National Herald wrote that a gunman used an AK-47 to shoot through bullet-resistant windows and finished him with a handgun, and called him arguably the most influential figure in the underworld since the shooting of his main rival, Vassilis Roubetis, in June 2023, in an ambush in the Korydallos district. In early March a blast wrecked a petrol station in Piraeus that Zampounis had once owned, which Greek media read as a message to his successor, Balkan Insight reported.

That January three suspects were taken before a public prosecutor, reported as ethnic Greeks from former Soviet countries and unnamed. According to Kathimerini, quoted by The National Herald, they were facing counts of murder, participation in a criminal organisation and attempted murder in connection with the killings of Zampounis, Roubetis and Yiannis Skaftouros, shot in May 2022. Eight more people had been identified, it said, two of them abroad and two in prison. Police were also looking at Russian gangsters linked to a group known as Vor V Zakone. These were suspects, not convicted men.

The latest killing in the sources was that of Giannis Lalas, described by The National Herald as a prominent figure in the night-time underworld. On 1 November 2025 he was ambushed at a chalet in Eptalofos, in the Delphi municipality, while on a balcony on a call, and shot eight times, two of them to the head, according to investigators cited by The National Herald. Police found the burned getaway car with a Kalashnikov inside it. In mid-November four people were detained in Thessaloniki and Kavala; Kathimerini's unnamed police sources described them as two Greeks and two ethnic Greeks from the former Soviet Union. Authorities ruled out a link to a previous attempted assassination in May, the report said.
content.h2: Police, prosecutors and the doubt over protection
content.p: Supreme Court Prosecutor Isidoros Dogiakos ordered an urgent inquiry in January 2023 into a report in the newspaper To Vima claiming that unnamed senior police officers shielded underworld bosses. The National Herald noted a year later that nothing more had been heard of it. The Organized Crime Index says allegations surfaced in 2024 that police officers had withheld key evidence in murder cases linked to the mafia, and that Greece's measures have mainly hit lower-tier actors. It also says Greece has declared a policy of "zero tolerance" toward organised crime.

The IPI reported that RSF ranks Greece last in the EU on its press freedom index, The National Herald wrote that only a few journalists write about the underworld because of the danger, and that two have been killed.
